title: Cell Viability vs. Total Cell Count

references.label: General microbiology/quantitative methods references (ASM, FDA BAM, CLSI)

summary: Total cell count measures how many cells (living and dead combined) are present in a sample, while viability measures what fraction of those cells are actually alive — two related but distinct measurements that together give a more complete picture of a culture's condition than either alone.
explanation: A dying culture can have a perfectly normal-looking total cell count while containing a large proportion of dead or dying cells, which would be missed by a raw count alone. Viability assays (such as trypan blue exclusion, which relies on an intact cell membrane excluding the dye while a compromised dead-cell membrane lets it in and stains the cell) distinguish live from dead cells within the same counted population, giving a viable cell count and a viability percentage alongside the total count. Both numbers matter for downstream work: total count for planning how many cells are available, and viability for judging whether the culture is healthy enough to use for a given application.

comparison.example: All cells counted regardless of condition — a hemocytometer count of every cell in the grid squares
Percentage of counted cells that exclude a dye like trypan blue (intact membrane, considered live) versus those that take up the dye (compromised membrane, considered dead)

commonMisconceptions: Assuming a normal total cell count means the culture is healthy, without checking viability.

Treating a viability assay based on membrane integrity as a perfect proxy for full cell health — a cell can have an intact membrane yet be metabolically compromised in ways that membrane-exclusion dyes do not detect.
